claims.text: AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock has a typical particle morphology and composition used in metallic additive manufacturing.
A picosecond-range laser with pulse energies of approximately 10–100 μJ is an applicable replacement for a continuous-wave laser in AlCrFeNiSi additive manufacturing.
Ultrashort laser pulses localize melting to a confined region.
Localized melting under ultrashort pulses minimizes thermal diffusion into surrounding material.
Rapid localized melting and solidification produce an ultra-fine microstructure.
Rapid localized melting and solidification markedly reduce the heat-affected-zone width.
Ultrashort pulses deposit energy through nonlinear absorption.
Confined ultrashort-pulse energy deposition promotes dynamic recrystallization.
The proposed microstructural refinement and reduced thermal diffusion lower residual thermal stresses.
Ultrashort-pulse-processed parts will have higher yield strength than continuous-wave-processed parts.
Ultrashort-pulse-processed parts will have greater ductility than continuous-wave-processed parts.
Ultrashort-pulse processing will decrease post-processing complexity relative to conventional processing.
Conventional high-thermal-load continuous-wave laser additive manufacturing produces extensive heat-affected zones.
Conventional high-thermal-load continuous-wave laser additive manufacturing produces increased residual stresses.
Conventional high-thermal-load continuous-wave laser additive manufacturing produces coarser microstructures.

The proposed processing window is an inert atmosphere, miniature components of 1–10 mm, picosecond-range pulses at approximately 10–100 μJ, and high scanning speeds adjusted for low net thermal input.
The expected benefits may not extend to larger geometries or modified processing parameters.
